However, from the above discussions it is evident that the High Court Division committed no wrong in allowing the defendants application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint of Title Suit No. 42 of 1999 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. The parties of this subsequent Title Suit No. 42 of 1999 and the parties of earlier Title Suit No. 177 of 1994, are same, the subject matter of both these suits being the entire land of CS Plot No. 371 of CS Khatian 4300 'Ja' of Mouza-Shahar Dhaka, are same and also the issues raised and settled in the earlier suit and the issues for determination in the subsequent suit are same. The earlier suit was adjudicated on by a competent Court. In the circumstances the subsequent suit is barred by the principle of res-judicata as enunciated in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is true that where evidence is required to establish the plea of res judicata rejection of plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground of res-judicata cannot be approved. This Division expressed this view in an earlier case reported in 13 BLD (AD) 217. But where the statements of the very plaint disclose about the earlier suit and all other elements for constituting res-judicata there cannot be any bar in rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the present suit the plaint itself has supplied all the necessary materials which sufficiently show that the suit is barred by res-judicata. The plaintiff's plea that in the earlier suit the defendants obtained judgment in their favour by practicing fraud has been found false and baseless while dealing with the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the circumstances allowing the suit to proceed will not only be abuse of process of Court, but it will also be defence of mandatory provision of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This provision of law clearly bars the present suit. So the High Court Division rightly allowed the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and rightly rejected the plaint of subsequent suit. We find nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment of the High Court Division.

paragraph: 21. Now, it is necessary to see who is a “co-sharer tenant of land” and what has been meant by “co-sharer tenant in the holding”. Generally co-sharer means joint owners (in Bengali what is called “শরিক বা শরিক প্রজা”).When the term is used in respect of property it means-‘a person who shares his right, title and interest with some other person(s) in a holding or plot or in an undivided share thereof. Land in connection with section 24 of the NAT Act, appears to be a plot or a parcel of plots owned by two or more co-sharers jointly. So, in order to exercise the right of pre-emption under the aforesaid Act, the person so claiming must be a co-sharer in an undivided plot or parcel thereof. Side by side it is also to be seen whether such co-sharership comes to an end, if so, how? In 54 DLR 181 case it has been observed that ‘the word land as used in section 24 of NAT Act should not mean the quantum of land in one plot only. As the word co-sharer always implies the existence of more than one person jointly owning, similarly, such joint ownership may be in respect of land in one plot or in several plots. The land is always recorded under a holding for the purpose of revenue record and payment of rents. This holding may be joint or of several persons. The holding of any land could only be sub divided and rents distributed in accordance with the procedure spelt out under section 117 of the SAT Act which will affect the land appertaining to such holding. A holding is popularly known as “Khatian” comprising of such land. The concept of co-sharer cannot be conceived independent of any holding or tenancy. If the holding is recorded in the name of more than one person then each of such person or their successors in interests becomes co-sharers to each other in such land. Such co-sharer will be deemed to continue as such co-owner in both holding as well as in land so long the holding will continue to be joint. Contrary to such proposition, that sub-division of such holding will not affect the land in any way is fallacious in as much as sub-division of the holding and creation of new plot in subsequent survey or by mutation by the acts of parties, the previous co-sharer in the holding and/or the land cannot be deemed to still continue as such co-sharer’.

The High Court Division failed to notice that a decree within the meaning of the Code of Civil Procedure means the formal expression of an adjudication conclusively determine the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may either be preliminary or final. In a suit for specific performance of contract, the court decides the controversy between the vendor and the vendee and direct the vendor to execute the deed in favour of the vendee if it is proved that the agreement is enforceable by law. It does not determine the title of the vendor in the property. It is true that in proviso to sub-section (l) of section 5 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1885, no particular type of decree or order passed by a civil court at any time before the publication of the list has been mentioned. There is a reference as to any decree order passed by a civil court before the publication of the list in the gazette, but in view of the inclusion of the words 'declaring the building not to be an abandoned property .... to have been vested in the government...' there is no doubt about the intention of the legislature that unless a competent civil court passed a decree declaring the non-abandoned character of the building, the listing of the same cannot be said illegal. It is thus clear that the list shall not include any building if the decree or order is found declaring the building not to be an abandoned property or not to have been vested in Government under PO 16 of 1972 or the possession by the Government of the building as abandoned property under that order to be illegal invalid or directing the Government or any officer or authority subordinate to it to return, restore or transfer the building to any person.

The first case of 1 BLC arose out of a judgment and order passed in a writ petition declaring the order of Additional Commissioner, Khulna Division dated 24-3-1988 in Redemption Appeal No.213 of 1985 "as of no legal effect." Facts of that case were that respondent No. 1 purchased one acre of land from the appellant by a registered kabala dated 24-6-1967 for a consideration of Taka 2,000. On the same date he executed a registered agreement to reconvey the kabala if the consideration money was repaid within 4 years from that date. A proceeding started by the appellant under the Act, 1950 for redemption of the kabala land vide Miscellaneous Case No.922BK /73-74 was dismissed by the Circle Officer (Revenue), Bakergonj by his order dated 3-2-1983 and appeal from the said order was also dismissed the Additional Deputy Commissioner Revenue) on 1-7-1985, upon a further appeal the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Khulna by his order dated 24-3-1988 allowed the appeal and ordered redemption of the land as prayed for by the appellant in his miscellaneous case which was set-aside by the High Court Division in the writ petition. Further facts were that the appellant also filed Miscellaneous Case No.1227 of 1972-73 before the then Sub-divisional Officer, Barisal (South) to get the land redeemed. During the pendency of the needing the appellant filed Title Suit No. 287 of 1979 in the Second Court of Munsif, Barisal for specific performance of contract on the basis of the aforesaid agreement for reconveyance which was dismissed on 17-4-1980 on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation. The appellant took an appeal, Title Appeal No. 120 1980, which was also dismissed by the District Judge, Bakergonj on 26-6-1981. In this context this Division dismissed the appeal on the view that the parties agreed to the transaction in question that the period of mortgage will be for 4 years beginning from 24-6-1967. So, the transaction cannot be alive and subsisting on the date of promulgation, of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972, i.e., 3-8-1972. It was a transaction past and closed. In this case, the view taken in 34 DLR (AD) 237 as quoted above was endorsed. The striking feature of the instant case and the case reported in 1 BLC (AD) 90 is that in the instant case a regular suit for redemption of the mortgaged land was filed, but in the reported case recourse was taken to the provisions of section 95 of the Act, 1950 after the promulgation of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 on 3-8-1972. The facts of the second case of 1 BLC are almost similar to the first case. And we consider it sufficient to say that in this case also no suit for redemption was filed and recourse was taken under the provisions of section 95 of the Act, 1950 after the expiry of the right of reconveyance of respondent No. 4 as per terms of the contemporaneous agreement which expired on 10-1-1972 and this Division allowed the appeal declaring the order passed by respondent No.1, Assistant Commissioner (Land), Lauhajang on 10-5-1992 directing the appellant to hand over possession of the disputed land to respondent No.4 to have been passed without lawful authority and be of no legal effect on the same view taken in the first case. The deed dated January 8, 1976 has been filed by the appellant before the Court of Assistant Judge in support of his claim as regard the property in respect where he has sought for declaration of title and confirmation of possession. The said document has been sent to the Hand Writing Expert or opinion and the report of the Hand Writing Expert yet to be received by the said Court and as such the genuineness or otherwise of the said deed in the background of pendency of the Title Suit awaits adjudication. This shows that the deed in question has been used by the appellant in the Title Suit and would be relied upon by the appellant as piece of evidence in support the claim being the subject matter of the Title Suit No. 62 of 1993. Even if on the termination of trial of the Title Suit the document in question is found by the court otherwise than being genuine then also Respondent No. 2 under the law would not be competent to initiate criminal proceeding on the allegation deed in question is forged as has been given in evidence in the trial. In view of the provision of clause (c) of section 195(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Respondent No. 2 may approach the court for taking appropriate step against the appellant since he used a deed in the suit as genuine inspite of knowing the same being forged and then it is for the court alone that may decide as to whether it would initiate proceeding against the appellant for committing one of the offence or more as mentioned in clause (c) of section 195 (1) Cr. paragraph: 2. The plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of right, title and interest in the suit land and for recovery of khas possession by evicting the defendant no.1 therefrom stating, inter alia, that the suit land along with its northern 1380 sq. fit appertaining to the settlement plot No. 7808 and Municipal holding No. 884 of Sylhet Municipality originally belonged to Birendra Lal Das and others popularly known as "Lal Brothers" in their Maliki right, one Sital Proshad Choube was a lessee under them in respect of that land. After taking lease from them he constructed a shop house and residential quarters over the land and possessed the same accordingly. He then gifted the land and the structure standing thereon to his grand sons Durga Proshad Tribedi and Mahabir Proshad Tribedi equally by a registered deed of gift dated 21.1.1927. On the basis of this gift Tribedi brothers began to own and possess the premises equally in ejmali as lessees under Lal Brothers. At the time of the gift Mahabir was minor and used to live with his elder brothers Durga Proshad who later on constructed new houses by removing the old one at his own cost and provided therein electric connection, water line, etc. Tribedi brothers continued to own and possess the premises in ejmali and there was no partition between them at any point of time. After the expiry of the lease they apprehended ejectment by Lal Brothers. So, they executed a registered kabala dated 27.3.1942 in favour of Kanailal Surma and his brothers. Then Lal Brothers brought a suit for ejectment being Title Suit No. 169 of 1944 in the First Court of Munsif, Sadar, Sylhet against the Tribedi Brothers. During the pendency of that ejectment suit Mahabir executed a kabala dated 4.4.1944 in favour of Harendra Nath Chakravorty for his 8 annas share though he had no saleable interest in the property at the relevant time. This kabala dated 4.4.1944 is a collusive document and it was never acted upon. Harendra Nath never claimed any right, title and possession on the basis of that kabala. Lal Brothers then obtained a decree in the ejectment suit on 6.4.1945 against the Tribedi Brothers and put the decree into execution being Execution Case No. 14 of 1946. But during the pendency this execution case, Kanailal Surama and others, on the basis of their kabala dated 27.3.1942 from Tribedi Brothers, filed Title Suit No. 29 of 1947 in the First Court of Sadar Munsif, Sylhet for declaration of their title and confirmation of possession over the premises against Lal Brothers impleading Durga Proshad Tribedi, Mahabir Proshad " Tribedi and Harendra Nath Chakraborty, but subsequently the name of Tribedi Brothers and Harendra Nath were struck off from the plaint and the suit was compromised on 9.7.1946 amongst Surmas and Lal Brothers, and thereby Surmas retained their right in the structures they purchased. In the said Title Execution Case No. 14 of 1946 Tribedi Brothers filed an objection being Misc. Case No. 145 of 1947 on 28.4.1947 wherein they asserted that they are not liable to be rejected as per provisions of Sylhet Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act of 1947 as they completed 12 years of possession of the premises. Their contention was upheld upto the High Court in the 2nd   Appeal being Appeal No. 14 of 1947 vide judgment dated 9.12.1952 and it was decided that the Tribedi Brothers had a protected interest and they were not liable to be ejected. Mahabir Proshad Tribedi then executed and registered a Nadabi Patra dated 18.1.1956 in favour of Lal Brothers in respect of his 8 annas share in the property. This Nadabipatra is a collusive document. After execution of this document by Mahabir Durga Proshad filed a case for pre-emption being Misc. Case No. 116 of 1956 under section 24 of the E.B. Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act in the 1st Court of Sadar Munsif, Sylhet in order to save the property from further burbles. That case was allowed in part on 24.8.1956. Durga Proshad then preferred Misc. Appeal No. 119 of 1957 in the Court of District Judge, Sylhet. The present defendant No.2 also preferred another Misc. Appeal being Misc. Appeal No. 126 of 1957 against the said order dated 24.8.1957 passed by the learned Munsif. The appellate Court allowed the Misc. Appeal No. 119 of 1957 and dismissed the Misc. Appeal No. 126 of 1957 on 13.11.1958. Thereafter two revision cases numbering C.R. 1301 and 1302 of 1958 were preferred before the High Court where in was held that no transfer was effected by the said Nadabipatra vide judgment dated 21.1.1959. In the meantime Lal Brothers created a kabala in favour of the defendant no.2 showing the sale of 8 annas share in the property. But in spite of all this maneuvers neither Harendra Nath nor Lal Brothers nor the defendant no. 2 ever acquired any right, title, interest or possession in the property. paragraph: 14. The plaintiffs are claiming the land in suit on the basis of inheritance and their said case was not established and the Court of first instance as well as the appellate Court on consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary held that the plaintiffs failed to establish their case in respect of the land in suit. In the afore state of the matter observation of the appellate Court was not only legally well conceived one but also was not consonant with the finding made by it on consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary the finding of the Court of first instance as well as of the appellate Court being that plaintiffs failed to establish their claim in respect of the land in suit or in other words could not prove their case and the said finding being based on the materials on record and the High Court division having had not disturbed the said finding as well as the finding that the suit was bad since same was filed against dead person the order of remand made by the High Court Division with the direction to the trial Court to hear the suit afresh upon giving opportunity to the parties to adduce further evidence, "if it is at all necessary " and also to consider the evidence on record afresh " without prejudice to any party" was not legally well founded one since the suit was filed against dead persons and consequently the suit in respect of throes persons being not maintainable and that as the plaintiffs failed to establish their claim in respect of the land in suit, they were not entitled to the relief and consequently the suit as was liable to be dismissed and as such the Court of first instance as well as the appellate Court in dismissing the suit did not commit any error. The finding and decision of the courts below relates to the subject matter of the suit in its entirety and that being the position, the defendants, non-calming the fraction of the land in suit. i.e. 80 acre of land (defendants kahuliyat relates to 68.20 acres of land) does not establish claim of the plaintiffs in respect of the said quantity of land since concurrent finding of the courts below were that plaintiffs failed to prove their case or in other words failed to establish their claim in respect of 69 acres of land which also includes the land not claimed by the defendants. In that state of the matter observation of the appellate Court for ascertaining the land of the R.S. khatians and of making gratuitous advice to the plaintiffs to bring fresh suit for establishing their claim in respect of the remaining land, that is the land outside the land of the defendants kabuliyat was quite beyond the frame of the suit. This being the position there was no occasion for remanding the suit back to the trial Court for fresh adjudication and as such High Court Division was in error in making the order of remand. The uniform view of the superior Courts is that an order of remand is not legally sustainable while the same tantamount to fresh trial of the subject matter of the suit upon allowing a party in the suit, who was negligent in bringing on record the materials which were relevant for adjudication of the subject matter of the suit or in other words to allow a party to fill up the lacuna. The order of remand is also not sustainable in law while same gives an opportunity to a party in the suit to make fresh attempt on the basis of the order of remand to establish his claim in respect of the subject matter of the suit which he earlier failed.

Thereafter the petitioner prayed before the Secretary, Ministry of Defence for mutation of her name, but that prayer was rejected with a direction upon this petitioner to file a regular suit before the court of law. After death of Kasirun Nessa Chowdhury and her husband, the suit land devolved on their son Mumik Hosan Chowdhury, defendant No. 2 and daughter Hamida Khatun Chowdhury, defendant No. 6, by way of inheritance. By amicable settlement, the suit land fell in the saham of Hamida Khatun Chowdhury. While possessing the suit land, she submitted her return as per provision of P.O. (President's Order) 98 of 1972. Hamida Khatun Chowdhury being issueless used to cultivate her land by bargadar. A portion of the suit land was being possessed by Niltak Barman by way of licence from her. On 02.10.1979, Enam Ali disclosed to Hamida Khatun that his two sons got lease of the suit land from the Government and as such, he would not pay the share of Barga and after the enquiry by her servant, she came to know that in her return she wrongly stated 3.06 acres of land in Plot No. 544 instead of the suit plot. Hamida Khatun filed a petition to the Revenue Officer for amendment and on 16.10.1979, Miscellaneous Case No.  XIII of 1979-80 was started and the notices were served upon the concerned parties. On 28.04.1980, the Revenue Officer, on receipt of the report of enquiry, amended the return inserting Plot No. 561 in place of Plot No. 544. After that, possession was taken over from leases by beating drum. While in possession of the suit land, Hamida Khatun sold the same to plaintiff Nos. 1-5 by registered deed of sale dated 13.04.1981. While plaintiff Nos. 1-5 have been possessing of the suit land, the brother of Hamida Khatun submitted return in the name Monalik Chowdhury, showing Plot No.  561 instead of Plot No. 544. Against the order of Revenue Officer, defendants filed an appeal to A.D.C (Additional Deputy Commissioner) (Revenue), who allowed the appeal setting aside the order of Revenue Officer. Subsequently, the plaintiffs filed an appeal against the order of A.D.C (Revenue) before the Land Appeal Board, which upheld the order of the A.D.C. (Revenue). During the pendency of the suit the defendant No. 1 filed additional written statement stating that the suit land originally belonged to Lal Mohmud, the proforma-defendant No.2 who, is the father of the plaintiff and he submitted two returns one in his own name and another in the name of his son, the plaintiff, who was a minor and a bachelor at the relevant time of his alleged purchase from his father and others and accordingly the Circle Officer (Rev), Nacho considered two returns as one return taking the view that the lands belonged to Lal Mahmud and accordingly the excess land vested in the government and then the possession of excess lands were taken by the government and was leased out to different persons in the year 1384 B.S, and those allottees are in possession of the suit land, Lal Mahmud, the father of the plaintiff, also filed separate suit being Other Class Suit No.66 of 1978, which was subsequently renumbered as 76 of 1982, and the same is pending before the same Court. After hearing the above Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1982 the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) decreed the suit. Being aggrieved Government of Bangladesh preferred the above First Appeal No. 149 of 1989 and the High Court Division, after hearing, dismissed the same holding that the father of the plaintiff had 4 wives and the mother of the plaintiff left the house of the father of the plaintiff and lived separately and the plaintiff had separate homestead having separate holding and he paid Union Parishad taxes against the said holding, which has not been denied and challenged by the defendant No.1 and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) dismissed the appeal of the plaintiff on the presumption that the plaintiff had no separate family before. 5 years from the promulgation of Bangladesh Laikl Holding Limitation Order, P.O. 98 of 1972, but the provision of section 2(b) of the above P.O. 98 of 1972 shows that such provisions of the definition of family i. e five years before 16th day December, 1971, has been amended by the words "before the 20th day of February, 1972 and as such the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), on misconception of law, dismissed the appeal of the plaintiff on 19.9.1977 fully knowing that such provisions has been amended by P.O. 154 of 1972; further the plaintiff, to prove his case, exhibited money receipts of payment of taxes of Union Parishad, kabinnama of the plaintiff, ration card of the plaintiff, rent receipts of the properties of the plaintiff, mutation khatian of the plaintiff, the registered deed Nos. 21401 dated 28.8.1969, 21960 dated 9.9.1969, 10516 dated 18.9.1969 in the name of the plaintiff and the trial Court after taking evidences found that the plaintiff is the head of his separate family since before 20.2.1972 and the trial Court rightly held that there is no provision that the plaintiff is to be a Head of separate family before five years from 16th day December, 1971 as the provision of section 2(b) shows that the person being an adult ant married who having been living in separate mess independently continuously since before 20th day of February, 1972 with his wife, son and others shall be deemed to be separate fairly and as such the plaintiff, being an adult and married and living in a separate mess from his parents along with his mother, sons and daughter, constitute a separate family and as suet the plaintiff is entitled to keep the properties as submitted in his return.

Nawab Ali, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing for the petitioner submitted that the Additional District Judge committed an error of land in not applying the settled principle of law that none but the contracting par-ties and the Government should be parties in the instant suit for specific performance of contract that the Additional District Judge committed an error of law in allowing the civil revision and application of the applicant No. 1-11 for addition as defendant in the suit on the ground of avoiding multiplicity of suits or proceedings in the face of his own finding that already there were suits between the applicants and defendants and the applicants lost the suits and appeals arising therefrom and the applicants preferred civil revision against the appellate decree and in not considering that the applicants are not entitled in law to agitate the question of title against the defendants at the trial stage of the instant suit. The learned Advocate finally submitted that in a suit for specific performance of contract a third party is not a necessary party whose presence before the Court is not necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the question in the suit and the petitioner is claiming spec if is performance for 0.18 acres of land whereas the applicants arc claiming 22½ acres of land. Mohammad ilasim died leaving behind 3 sons namely Jabid Ali, Sunahor Ali and Ajob Ali. 0.70 acres of land was recorded in the name of Abdul Latif and in separate Ichatian rest 0.12 acres and 0.02 acres of land had been recorded in the name of Jabid Ali and Abdul Latif respectively. Jabid Ali died leaving behind 3 sons namely Mubid Ali, Tojomul Ali and Tofozzul Ali and 2 daughters. Mubid Ali and Tojomul Ali on getting 2nd schedule land amicably in their share transferred the same in favour of Ijjad Ali vide registered kabala dated 16.10.1960 and delivered possessing thereof. Ijjad Ali transferred the said 2nd schedule land on 06.12.1962 in favour of Abdul Latif the predecessor of the plaintiff and delivered possession but as he died before executing the kabala his heirs subsequently executed and registered the said kabala. His heirs subsequently executed and registered the said kabala on 01.12.1985 in favour of plaintiffs and preform defendant Nos. 39 40. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 predecessor of defendant Nos. 10-13, Mokrom Ali, predecessor of defendant Nos. 14-19, Mosoddor Ali and one Moin Uddin and 6 persons mutated the suit land in their name against which plaintiff filed mutation appeal and then it was revealed that with the collusion of Mubid Ali the said 6 persons by creating a "Muktipatra" mutated their names. The suit land was finally recorded in the name of the plaintiffs and preform defendant Nos. 39-47. In the manner as stated the plaintiff and his co-sharer were owning and possessing the suit land. Defendant No. 1 by claiming the suit land of his own gave threat to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land which constrained the plaintiff to file a title suit being No. 25 of 2000 and during pendency of that suit on 19.06.2000 defendants forcibly dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land. The plaintiff had withdrawn the suit as there were some formal defects in framing the suit and then instituted the instant suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of the second schedule land. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter-alia, that second schedule land belonged to Jabid Ali who while owing and possessing the suit land executed and registered a lease deed on 02.12.1955 in favour of Joroi Ullah, the father of defendant Nos. 1 and 5 others. While Joroi Ullah and others were holding and possessing the suit land the same was recorded in the name of Jabid Ali and thereafter the heirs of Jabid Ali on 02.11.1982 executed and registered a "Muktipatra" in favour of the contesting defendant and thus the contesting defendant and their co-sharer mutated the suit land in their name and paid rent to the government. The plaintiff had preferred a mutation appeal and that was rejected on 15.03.1988. Moin Uddin and others sold out their share to the defendant No. 1 by a registered deed dated 04.01.1997 and delivered possession thereof. The suit land was recorded in the name of the defendant No. 1. The boundary as described in the plaint is incorrect and unspecified and without holding local investigation the plaintiff can not get any relief. With a view to causing loss to the defendant the plaintiff by withdrawing earlier suit instituted the instant suit with false claim as such he prayed for dismissal of the suit.
